11 A rigid uniform bar of length 2.4 m is pivoted horizontally at its midpoint.
0.8 m
0.8 m
200 N
300 N
Weights are hung from two points on the bar as shown in the diagram. To maintain equilibrium, a
couple is applied to the bar.
What is the torque and direction of this couple?
A
40 N m clockwise
B
40 N m anticlockwise
C
80 N m clockwise
D
80 N m anticlockwise

hints: Notice the pivot is at the midpoint of the $2.4\text{ m}$ bar, so each half is $1.2\text{ m}$ long - use this to find each weight's perpendicular distance from the pivot.

Connect the $0.8\text{ m}$ labels to distances from the pivot: the $200\text{ N}$ weight is $0.8\text{ m}$ left of the pivot, while the $300\text{ N}$ weight is $0.8\text{ m}$ from the right end and so $1.2 - 0.8 = 0.4\text{ m}$ right of the pivot.
Calculate clockwise moment $F \times d$ and anticlockwise moment $F \times d$ separately, then find the net resultant moment that the applied couple must cancel.
walkthrough: The uniform bar's weight acts at its midpoint, which is at the pivot, so it has zero moment about the pivot and can be ignored.

Find perpendicular distances: left $200\text{ N}$ weight is $0.8\text{ m}$ to the left of the pivot; right end is $1.2\text{ m}$ from the pivot, so the $300\text{ N}$ weight $0.8\text{ m}$ from the right end is $1.2 - 0.8 = 0.4\text{ m}$ to the right of the pivot.
Use moment $= F \times d$: left moment $= 200 \times 0.8 = 160\text{ N m}$ tending to turn the left side down, which is anticlockwise.
Right moment $= 300 \times 0.4 = 120\text{ N m}$ tending to turn the right side down, which is clockwise.
Resultant moment $= 160 - 120 = 40\text{ N m}$ anticlockwise. For equilibrium the resultant moment must be zero, so the couple must supply $40\text{ N m}$ clockwise. This is option A.

A.explanation: The net moment is $40\text{ N m}$ anticlockwise, so a $40\text{ N m}$ clockwise couple restores zero resultant moment.

B.explanation: This has the correct magnitude but would add to the existing anticlockwise resultant instead of balancing it.

C.explanation: This uses $0.8\text{ m}$ for both weights, giving $300 \times 0.8 - 200 \times 0.8 = 80\text{ N m}$, ignoring that the $300\text{ N}$ weight is only $0.4\text{ m}$ from the pivot.

D.explanation: This both uses the wrong $0.8\text{ m}$ distance for the $300\text{ N}$ weight and acts in the same sense as the resultant moment.
